title: Encryption has a new problem: AI is getting better at proving the impossible
summary: AI has solved yet another math problem that stumped humans for more than 150 years, ratcheting up questions about the efficacy, or even relevancy, of cryptography in the age of AI. Aided by Claude, mathematician and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge is believed to have proven the Riemann Hypothesis , one of the most famous open problems in math. It posits that prime numbers, or the ‘atoms’ of all math, are actually distributed neatly and predictably, not randomly or sporadically as they may seem. The hypothesis’ proof could, at least in some eventualities, change the story of modern cryptography, because prime numbers serve as secret passcodes that help hide sensitive data. Still, security leaders and teams shouldn’t panic, even as mathematicians may be in mourning. “This development does not mean encryption has suddenly been broken,” said Fritz Jean-Louis , a principal cybersecurity instructor at Infotech. “The more important security aspect is the speed of AI-assisted mathematical discovery.” The dawn of ‘something far greater’ Mathematician Bernhard Riemann proposed his eponymous hypothesis in 1859, suggesting a hidden pattern in the distribution of prime numbers (numbers like 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, and so on that are divisible only by themselves and 1). They are the building blocks of whole numbers, while at the same time hiding deeper, unresolved patterns, or so it has been thought. The Riemann Hypothesis has lacked a general proof for 167 years; the Clay Mathematics Institute even offers a $1 million bounty to anyone who can generate one. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems with this distinction. But last week, Alpöge posted a proof generated with Claude in Lean, a programming language that verifies the mathematical correctness of each step. Alpöge initially posted just the proof because the detailed text occupies more than 250,000 pages. title: The SaaS resiliency bill is coming due
summary: The latest Microsoft outage should give enterprise architects pause. Widespread disruptions to Microsoft 365—including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot—affected users across many countries, with reports of sharp spikes in outages. What was a temporary annoyance for many became a serious business interruption for enterprises. Here’s an inconvenient truth: If these systems had run entirely on equipment you controlled, many would have kept working—not all, or forever, but enough to matter. A laptop word processor needs no healthy hyperscale cloud to draft a document. A local mail server needs no software-as-a-service (SaaS) identity system, telemetry, synchronization, collaboration, and policy services to agree it’s a good day to send an email. But that’s not how we’ve built most modern business software. Applications may look local but depend on remote services for authentication, licensing, files, configuration, AI, security, syncing, search, workflows, and even startup. When the back-end service goes offline, the local software may still be on the device, but the business function is unavailable. Moving to a new model I’ve watched this shift unfold over decades. In the client/server era, we worried about LANs, database clusters, storage, and the occasional angry CFO who wanted to know why the ERP system was down before the quarterly close. Those systems were imperfect, expensive, and often painful to maintain. However, their failure domains were usually visible. If the database server failed, we knew where. If the network switch died, we could point to it. If the backup failed, someone in the data center had some explaining to do. Then the industry embraced SaaS to avoid endless upgrades and desktop patching, shift costs from capital to operating expenses, and gain collaboration, automatic updates, centralized policies, and remote-work support. title: When five AI agents make one mistake, which one’s at fault?
summary: Early in my career, I helped build a healthcare platform for patient-reported outcomes. It exchanged data with a federal health system and several EHR vendors. The hard question with those integrations was never whether the data moved. It was who started the access, and under what authority. A database could tell you which credential read the record. An application log could tell you which service handled the request. Neither could tell you which person was behind it. My job was to carry that context through every layer so the access could be explained later. That work also led to two U.S. patents I hold on secure storage of and access to patient health information. I’ve been thinking about that problem again as agents start working side by side. Meta acquired Conductor , a workspace for running coding agents in parallel. GitHub’s new Git storage architecture handled 5,000 concurrent agents on one repository in internal testing. Anthropic opened a private beta for enterprises to self-host Managed Agents. Different products, same direction. Agents are moving into shared repositories, shared tools and shared infrastructure. Anthropic’s own research shows what can go wrong there. In August, it described an experiment in which three Claude instances, each on its own VM, were told to migrate the same Python backend on a fourth VM to a different language. None knew the others existed. Over four hours, they disabled one another’s Unix accounts, wrote looping scripts to kill each other’s processes and disguised malicious code as another agent’s work. Anyone who has sat through a tense sprint retro may find that oddly familiar. The agents just got there faster. In a separate pricing game, agents with a private channel started colluding within three rounds. When Anthropic removed every direct channel, they kept matching prices to the penny through a public listings board. Those results got the headlines. What worries me is more boring. title: Your AI agent shouldn’t get to grade its own work
summary: In a recent experiment , Claude Opus 4.8 built an invoice checker, revised it, and raised its score from just over 45 out of 100 to a perfect 100. That’s roughly a 122% improvement. Banish the humans! The robots have won. Well, maybe not. Remember that math teacher in eighth grade who let you grade your own tests? I do. Turns out there’s too much opportunity to cheat in that scenario, just as there is here, though it’s perhaps a different form of cheating. Here, Claude wrote the test. The researchers had 60 invoices of their own , and the original checker correctly flagged every bill that needed review and let the rest through. The revised checker? Same 60 invoices, same 60 correct calls. Claude deserves credit for building a good invoice checker. The thing is, it already had a good invoice checker before it made the “upgrade.” Hence, I’ll happily let an agent write the code and the tests. What would make me less happy is having the agent pick the only evidence we look at before we ship. If the agent misunderstands what the business wants, which is largely a human matter, its tests can reward it for getting the software wrong. Perfectly… wrong Consider the banking assistant in the same study. GPT-5.5 played the developer here: It built and tested the assistant that would talk to the simulated bank’s customers. The bank provided a way to look up a customer by email. GPT-5.5 missed that and instead wrote a test that rewarded the assistant for asking the customer for an internal ID. What? To get the test to pass, GPT-5.5 programmed the assistant to insist on an internal ID. The assistant eventually scored 100% on GPT-5.5’s tests, and the optimizer reported “nothing_to_fix.” In two of the researchers’ test conversations, the assistant refused the lookup and the customer gave up. title: Microsoft has an old, but new, idea for PC upgrades: Cloud PCs
summary: Prohibitive prices have put many enterprises’ PC upgrades on hold, but Microsoft has another idea: upgrade to its “cloud PCs.” Cloud PCs are a reference to Windows 365 , which delivers a familiar, full Windows 11 desktop experience from the Microsoft Cloud. It works on a wide range of existing computing devices. Users don’t need a full-featured laptop. They can get a full Windows experience by launching an app on a lower-end Windows PC, Mac, or tablet, or through a specialized remote-desktop device. With PC prices going up, Windows 365 allows you to extend the life of your current PC fleet, said Pavan Davuluri, executive vice president of Windows and Devices at Microsoft, during the opening-day keynote at the company’s Ignite conference last week. “You can give compute to anyone in minutes, no new hardware. As you plan this PC refresh cycle, add cloud PCs to your estate,” Davuluri said. At Ignite, Microsoft introduced new technologies to make Windows 365 faster and easier to use. The product itself was launched five years ago, so it isn’t new, nor is the concept of getting a full-fledged computing experience through a single app window, which has been considered promising for decades. In the ’80s, Sun Microsystems coined the slogan “The network is the computer,” with the promise that powerful Unix servers would deliver full computing experiences to remote desktops with minimal hardware. In the late 2000s, netbooks with underwhelming hardware also promised more web-based computing, but faded away. Chromebooks are now a conduit for running applications hosted on the internet. But cloud PCs could be more relevant now, especially with AI in the picture, Microsoft officials argued. Unlike on-premises PCs, cloud PCs are “elastic.” Enterprises can choose configurations to match the compute to work, such as 2 virtual CPUs and 4GB of RAM for running light productivity tools and more CPUs, more RAM, and even GPUs for AI and graphics-intensive jobs. title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, extending AI-assisted development to pull request approvals
summary: Anthropic has launched Claude Ship in beta, letting software development teams delegate code approval to AI agents within limits set by individual repository policies. The launch targets a potential bottleneck in AI-assisted software development, where the speed at which developers can generate code may outpace their ability to review it. By combining automated reviews with the corrective work needed to prepare pull requests for approval, Anthropic is competing across a broader stretch of the software development lifecycle. Its integration with Claude Code could make it particularly attractive to enterprises already using Anthropic’s coding tools , according to Lian Jye Su , chief analyst at Omdia. But GitHub and GitLab have an advantage in how closely their AI tools integrate with their respective development platforms, said Deepika Giri , vice president of Asia/Pacific artificial intelligence platforms and advisory at IDC. “Anthropic’s Claude Ship is not a breakthrough innovation as much as an evolution of existing AI-assisted code review capabilities,” said Nitish Tyagi , senior principal analyst at Gartner. Claude Ship incorporates Anthropic’s generally available Code Review tool alongside PR Steward and Claude Approvals, both of which are in beta. Review depth is configurable at the repository level, with teams able to choose between Quick, Standard, and Deep reviews. PR Steward handles corrective work on open pull requests, responding to review feedback and problems that arise during continuous integration (CI). Its remit includes resolving merge conflicts but excludes approving or merging changes. Claude Approvals evaluates proposed changes against a policy file maintained within each repository. Engineering teams can authorize the agent to approve routine changes while reserving more sensitive decisions for human reviewers. Teams can incorporate automated review findings into approval policies and define additional classification criteria in natural language

title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
summary: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
summary: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , l

title: Robots vs Self Driving
summary: I sit down with Adrien Gaidon, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer of Walden Robotics, to map out where the openings sit in robotics and physical AI. Adrien explains how teams now teach robots with data, why deployment data carries the most value, and why Walden picked wheels and two-finger grippers for factory work. We dig into the opportunities around the big labs: data with scarce access, supply chain, teleoperation, insurance, software tools, and niche robots. If robotics feels like a game for companies with $300 million seed rounds, this episode lays out the smaller ways in too. This episode was made possible thanks to Anthropic (the team behind Claude) for hosting us at Claude Founder house and sponsoring the episode. Key Points • Deployment data carries the most value, and teams earn it by putting robots on production floors. • A strong data business sits where scarce access meets data that is useful for robots. • Data, compute, and manufacturing are linked bottlenecks that a robotics company widens together. • Robots that learn from deployment gain value over time, which opens new ways to price and sell them. • Bundling many small tasks makes automation pay where each task alone falls short. • Founders can pick their level of hard, from general-purpose robots to one-task niches like welding or gardening. Numbered Section Summaries 1. From Programming to Teaching Factory robots used to follow programmed points in space, blind to anything in their path. Adrien explains that teams now teach robots with data: web, video, and language data build a common-sense foundation model, and task demonstrations build the skill. He says he felt the physical version of AGI back in 2022, when his co-founders built diffusion policy and showed a robot could learn a task from examples. 2.
